name: Morehouse College
kind: Private HBCU · Men's liberal arts college
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society (historic); Baptist
description: Founded in 1867 in Augusta as the Augusta Institute to educate formerly enslaved men for ministry and teaching, the school moved to Atlanta in 1879 as Atlanta Baptist Seminary and took the Morehouse name in 1913. It is the nation's only historically Black college for men and the alma mater of Martin Luther King Jr. Its graduates have shaped Atlanta's Black business and political class — from Sweet Auburn newspaper founder W. A. Scott II and realtor Q. V. Williamson to Mayor Maynard Jackson, Godfather's Pizza CEO Herman Cain and filmmaker-entrepreneur Spike Lee.

facts.d: Began in 1867 at Springfield Baptist Church in Augusta before relocating to Atlanta in 1879.
Morehouse remains the only historically Black college in the U.S. exclusively for men.
Alumni include Atlanta's first Black mayor (Maynard Jackson, 1956), Sen. Raphael Warnock (1991) and a long line of Atlanta business figures.

name: Spelman College
kind: Private HBCU · Women's liberal arts college
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society (historic); Baptist
description: Founded in 1881 in the basement of Atlanta's Friendship Baptist Church by New England missionaries Sophia B. Packard and Harriet E. Giles as the Atlanta Baptist Female Seminary, it was renamed for the Spelman family (in-laws of John D. Rockefeller, its early benefactor) and became Spelman College in 1924. It is consistently ranked the top HBCU and is the nation's leading producer of Black women who go on to STEM doctorates. Alumnae include Walgreens CEO Rosalind Brewer, Children's Defense Fund founder Marian Wright Edelman and Stacey Abrams.

facts.d: John D. Rockefeller's support led the school to adopt the name of his wife Laura Spelman's family in 1884.
Rosalind Brewer (chemistry, 1984) became CEO of Sam's Club and Walgreens Boots Alliance and later chaired Spelman's board.
One of only two remaining historically Black colleges for women (with Bennett College).

name: Clark Atlanta University
description: Clark Atlanta University was formed in 1988 by the consolidation of Atlanta University (founded 1865, the first graduate institution serving African Americans) and Clark College (founded 1869 by the Methodist Freedmen's Aid Society). It is a Carnegie R2 research university in the Atlanta University Center with strong programs in business, mass media and the sciences. Its lineage produced Atlanta Life president Norris Herndon, Black Swan Records founder Harry Pace and Coca-Cola executive Carl Ware, and more recently media and music entrepreneurs such as Kenya Barris and DJ Drama.

facts.d: Atlanta University and Clark College merged in 1988 to form CAU.
Recent alumni include Black-ish creator Kenya Barris and Generation Now label co-founders DJ Drama and Don Cannon.
Diversity-management pioneer R. Roosevelt Thomas Jr. led its business school from 1979.

name: Atlanta University
affiliation: American Missionary Association; Freedmen's Bureau (early aid)
fate: Merged with Clark College in 1988 to form Clark Atlanta University.
description: Founded in 1865 with support from the American Missionary Association, Atlanta University grew from the Storrs School into a normal school and college, then from 1929–30 became an exclusively graduate institution — the first in the nation to serve African Americans — affiliated with Morehouse and Spelman. W. E. B. Du Bois taught there, and its alumni include James Weldon Johnson, Walter White, Lucy Craft Laney, Atlanta Life president Norris Herndon and Black Swan Records founder Harry Pace. Its business school trained international executives such as MTN Group's Phuthuma Nhleko and Nigeria's Oskar Ibru.

facts.d: Became an all-graduate institution around 1929–30, the first to serve African Americans.
W. E. B. Du Bois taught there, and Harry Pace (class of 1903) went into printing with him after graduating.
Phuthuma Nhleko (later CEO of MTN Group) and Oskar Ibru (later chairman of the Ibru Organisation) earned MBAs there.

name: Clark College
fate: Merged with Atlanta University in 1988 to form Clark Atlanta University.
description: Founded in 1869 by the Freedmen's Aid Society of the Methodist Episcopal Church and named for Bishop Davis W. Clark, the school operated as Clark University before being renamed Clark College in 1940 when it moved next to the Atlanta University Center. It was known for journalism and teacher education. Alumni include Coca-Cola executive Carl Ware, Congressman Hank Johnson, educator Marva Collins and early Atlanta businessman Luther Judson Price.

facts.d: Founded in 1869 by the Methodist Episcopal Church's Freedmen's Aid Society.
Carl Ware (B.A., political science) rose to executive vice president of the Coca-Cola Company.

name: Morris Brown College
description: Founded on January 5, 1881 by the AME Church's North Georgia Annual Conference, Morris Brown was the first educational institution in Georgia owned and operated entirely by African Americans. After losing its regional accreditation in 2002 over misuse of federal funds, it nearly closed, but regained accreditation through TRACS in 2022. Alumni include civil rights leader and businessman Hosea Williams and Atlanta's first Black woman police chief, Beverly Harvard.

facts.d: First Georgia educational institution founded and run entirely by African Americans.
Unaccredited from 2003 to 2022; now accredited by the Transnational Association of Christian Colleges and Schools.
Payne College of Cuthbert, Georgia became part of Morris Brown in 1912.

name: Payne College (Cuthbert)
fate: Became part of Morris Brown University on June 5, 1912.
description: Payne College was a small AME-affiliated school founded in 1879 in Cuthbert, in southwest Georgia. It operated until 1912, when it was absorbed into Morris Brown in Atlanta. It is distinct from Paine College in Augusta.

facts.d: On June 5, 1912 it became part of Morris Brown University.

name: Interdenominational Theological Center
kind: Private HBCU · Graduate theological seminary consortium
affiliation: Ecumenical (Baptist, United Methodist, AME, CME, COGIC and others)
description: The ITC was chartered in 1958 as a joint venture of four seminaries — Morehouse School of Religion (Baptist), Gammon Theological Seminary (United Methodist), Turner Theological Seminary (AME) and Phillips School of Theology (CME) — later joined by the Charles H. Mason Theological Seminary (COGIC) and others. It occupied the Gammon campus until its own buildings opened in 1961 and has trained a large share of Black clergy in the U.S.

facts.d: Founded in 1958 by Morehouse School of Religion, Gammon, Turner and Phillips seminaries.
Used the Gammon campus until its own facilities were completed in 1961.

name: Gammon Theological Seminary
affiliation: Methodist Episcopal Church / United Methodist Church
fate: Became a founding constituent seminary of the Interdenominational Theological Center (chartered 1958); ITC occupied its campus.
description: Gammon grew out of Clark University's theology department and became an independent Methodist seminary in 1883, named for benefactor Elijah H. Gammon. In 1958–59 it joined three other Black seminaries to form the Interdenominational Theological Center, which was built on the Gammon campus. Civil rights leader and SCLC president J. D. Grier earned his divinity degree there in 1956.

facts.d: Began as the theology department of Clark University (later Clark College).
One of the four seminaries that founded the ITC in 1958.

connections.label: spun out of Clark University theology dept.

name: Morehouse School of Medicine
formerNames: Medical Education Program at Morehouse College
description: Established in 1975 as a two-year medical education program at Morehouse College under founding dean Louis W. Sullivan, it became independent in 1981 and began awarding M.D. degrees. It focuses on primary care and health equity in underserved communities; former U.S. Surgeons General David Satcher (president) and Regina Benjamin (second graduating class) are tied to it.

facts.d: Began in 1975 as a program of Morehouse College and became independent in 1981.
Regina Benjamin was in its second graduating class; David Satcher later led the school.

name: Albany State University
formerNames: Albany Bible and Manual Training Institute
description: Founded in 1903 by Joseph Winthrop Holley as the Albany Bible and Manual Training Institute, the school became a state-supported normal and agricultural college in 1917 and is now part of the University System of Georgia. After absorbing (non-HBCU) Darton State College in 2017, it is the largest historically Black institution in Georgia. Olympian Alice Coachman earned her degree there.

facts.d: Joseph Winthrop Holley, son of formerly enslaved parents, founded it in 1903.
Following its 2017 consolidation with Darton State College, it is Georgia's largest HBCU.

name: Fort Valley State University
formerNames: Fort Valley High and Industrial School
description: Fort Valley State College was created in 1939 by consolidating the Fort Valley High and Industrial School (chartered 1896) with the State Teachers and Agricultural College for Negroes in Forsyth. Designated Georgia's land-grant college for Black students in 1949, it became a university in 1996 and is known for agriculture and veterinary technology. Atlanta civic and business leader Thomas W. Dortch Jr. and longtime legislator and Synovus executive Calvin Smyre are alumni.

facts.d: Formed from the Fort Valley High and Industrial School and the Forsyth State Teachers and Agricultural College.
Took over Georgia's 1890 land-grant role from Savannah State in 1947–49.

name: State Teachers and Agricultural College for Negroes
kind: Public HBCU · Teachers and agricultural college (defunct)
affiliation: American Missionary Association (early funding); University System of Georgia (from 1932)
formerNames: School of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts for the Training of Negroes
fate: Closed in 1938 and consolidated into the new Fort Valley State College in 1939; its campus became the Hubbard Training School.
description: Founded in 1902 by Rev. William Merida Hubbard as the Forsyth Normal and Industrial School with early help from the American Missionary Association, it was accredited in 1918 as Georgia's first vocational school for Black students. It became a public teachers college in 1931 and one of three Black public colleges added to the University System of Georgia in 1932, before the state merged it into Fort Valley State in 1939.

facts.d: Accredited in 1918 as the first vocational training school for African Americans in Georgia.
Consolidated into Fort Valley State College in 1939.

sources.label: Wikipedia — State Teachers and Agricultural College for Negroes (Georgia)

name: Paine College
affiliation: Christian Methodist Episcopal Church; United Methodist Church
description: Paine was founded on November 1, 1882 as a joint project of the Colored (now Christian) Methodist Episcopal Church and the white Methodist Episcopal Church, South — an unusual biracial partnership in the post-Reconstruction South. After SACS revoked its regional accreditation in 2016 amid financial problems, it is now accredited by TRACS. Alumni include novelist Frank Yerby, SCLC co-founder Joseph Lowery and Georgia Labor Commissioner Michael Thurmond.

facts.d: Founded by the CME Church together with the Methodist Episcopal Church, South.
Lost SACS accreditation in 2016; now accredited by TRACS.

name: Haines Normal and Industrial Institute
kind: Private HBCU · Normal and industrial school (defunct)
affiliation: Presbyterian Board of Missions for Freedmen
fate: Closed in 1949, years after founder Lucy Craft Laney's death; its site later housed Lucy C. Laney High School.
description: Lucy Craft Laney, a member of Atlanta University's first class, opened the school in Augusta in 1883 and secured backing from the northern Presbyterian Church; it was named for benefactor Francine E. H. Haines. Primarily a normal (teacher-training) and secondary institution, it trained generations of Black teachers in Georgia. Harry Pace taught there after graduating from Atlanta University, and novelist Frank Yerby graduated from it in 1933.

facts.d: Lucy Craft Laney (Atlanta University normal course, 1873) led it for 50 years.
Supported by the Presbyterian church after Laney appealed at its 1886 national convention.

sources.label: Georgia Historical Society — Haines Normal and Industrial Institute marker
New Georgia Encyclopedia — Lucy Craft Laney

name: Georgia Baptist College
kind: Private HBCU · Baptist college and grade school (defunct)
fate: Struggled financially for decades, went into foreclosure in 1937 and closed in 1956.
description: Central City College was founded in Macon in 1899 as a Black-led alternative to the white-run ABHMS schools such as Atlanta Baptist Seminary (Morehouse), spearheaded by Savannah Baptist leader Emanuel K. Love, with former Atlanta Baptist instructor William E. Holmes as first president. It operated mainly as a primary and secondary school, added a college department in 1920, was renamed Georgia Baptist College in 1938, and closed in 1956.

facts.d: Created amid disputes over white control of ABHMS schools in Georgia.
First president William E. Holmes had taught at Atlanta Baptist (Morehouse) for 25 years.

name: Savannah State University
formerNames: Georgia State Industrial College for Colored Youth
description: Created by the Georgia General Assembly on November 26, 1890 under the Second Morrill Act as the Georgia State Industrial College for Colored Youth, it is the oldest public HBCU in Georgia. Founding president Richard R. Wright Sr. led it for three decades before founding a bank in Philadelphia. It served as Georgia's Black land-grant college until 1947. Alumni include civil rights leader W. W. Law and Pro Football Hall of Famer turned media entrepreneur Shannon Sharpe.

facts.d: Chartered November 26, 1890; classes moved to Savannah in October 1891.
First president Richard R. Wright Sr. later founded Citizens and Southern Bank and Trust Co. in Philadelphia.

name: Herman Cain
hbcuStory: Graduated from Morehouse College in 1967 with a B.S. in mathematics, then earned a master's in computer science at Purdue while working for the U.S. Navy.
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Atlanta by a father who worked as a chauffeur for Coca-Cola president Robert Woodruff; his first corporate job was as a computer systems analyst at Coca-Cola.
breakthrough: After turning around 400 Burger King stores in the Philadelphia region for Pillsbury, he was named chairman and CEO of Godfather's Pizza in 1986, and led a buyout of the chain from Pillsbury in 1988.
legacy: Chaired the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (1995–96) and led the National Restaurant Association (1996–99) before a 2012 Republican presidential run; received the Horatio Alger Award in 1996.

breakthroughDetail.d: At 36 he was assigned to manage 400 Burger King stores around Philadelphia for Pillsbury.
Pillsbury made him chairman and CEO of Godfather's Pizza; he and fellow executives bought the chain from Pillsbury in 1988.
Chaired the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City's Omaha branch and later the bank itself.

legacyDetail.d: President and CEO of the National Restaurant Association, 1996–1999.
Received the award in 1996 and honorary degrees from Morehouse and others.

sources.label: NYT — Godfather's Pizza sold by Pillsbury (1988)

name: Walter E. Massey
hbcuStory: Entered Morehouse on a Ford Foundation early-admission fellowship as a teenager and graduated with a B.S. in 1958; returned in 1995 as the college's president.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Jim Crow–era Hattiesburg, Mississippi, where his math talent earned him a fellowship to Morehouse by mid-high school.
breakthrough: A physicist (Ph.D., Washington University), he directed Argonne National Laboratory and the National Science Foundation, then became chairman of Bank of America's board in 2009 during the financial crisis.
legacy: Led Morehouse (1995–2007) and the School of the Art Institute of Chicago; chairs the Giant Magellan Telescope board and has sat on numerous corporate boards.

breakthroughDetail.d: Served as chairman of the board of Bank of America.
Headed the National Science Foundation and Argonne National Laboratory.

legacyDetail.d: Returned to lead his alma mater from 1995 to 2007.

name: Spike Lee
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in mass communication from Morehouse in 1979 (taking film courses at Clark Atlanta), where he made his first student film, Last Hustle in Brooklyn; his father, jazz musician Bill Lee, also attended Morehouse.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Atlanta and raised in Brooklyn by a jazz-musician father and a teacher mother.
breakthrough: Founded 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks (with Monty Ross) and broke through with the micro-budget She's Gotta Have It (1986), followed by Do the Right Thing (1989) and Malcolm X (1992).
legacy: 40 Acres and a Mule has produced more than 35 films; Lee has won an Academy Award, two Emmys and three Peabodys, and helped open Hollywood doors for a generation of Black filmmakers.

breakthroughDetail.d: 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks has produced all of his films — more than 35 titles.
His NYU thesis film Joe's Bed-Stuy Barbershop: We Cut Heads won a Student Academy Award.

legacyDetail.d: By producing through his own company he retained creative and financial control of his catalog.

sources.label: Wikipedia — 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks

name: Maynard Jackson
hbcuStory: Entered Morehouse early and graduated in 1956 at age 18; his mother and all five aunts were Spelman graduates.
humbleBeginnings: Grandson of Sweet Auburn leader John Wesley Dobbs; his father was a Baptist minister.
breakthrough: Elected in 1973 as Atlanta's first Black mayor (and the first of any major Southern city), he required minority participation in city contracts, notably the Hartsfield airport expansion.
legacy: Served three terms (1974–82, 1990–94); founded the municipal bond firm Jackson Securities; the Atlanta airport now bears his name.

breakthroughDetail.d: Greatly increased minority business participation in city contracting, including the airport's expansion.

legacyDetail.d: Founded the investment firm Jackson Securities after leaving office.
Atlanta's airport was renamed in his honor in 2003.

name: Q. V. Williamson
hbcuStory: Graduated from Morehouse in 1940 with a business administration degree; later taught at Atlanta University.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Atlanta and educated at Booker T. Washington High School.
breakthrough: Built Q. V. Williamson & Company, a real estate brokerage, and helped develop the Black middle-class Collier Heights neighborhood; in 1965 became the first Black member of Atlanta's Board of Aldermen since Reconstruction.
legacy: Chaired the National Association of Real Estate Brokers and co-chaired the Atlanta Negro Voters League, linking Black property ownership to political power.

breakthroughDetail.d: Involved in establishing Atlanta's Collier Heights, a planned Black middle-class neighborhood.
First Black Atlanta alderman since Reconstruction, elected as a Republican.

legacyDetail.d: Served as chairman and president of the National Association of Real Estate Brokers.

name: Theodore Colbert III
hbcuStory: Completed the Morehouse–Georgia Tech dual-degree engineering program in 1996 with B.S. degrees in interdisciplinary science and industrial and systems engineering.
humbleBeginnings: Started in Ford Motor Company's College Graduate Program in information technology after graduation.
breakthrough: Joined Boeing, rose to chief information officer, then CEO of Boeing Global Services, and in 2022 CEO of Boeing Defense, Space & Security.
legacy: One of the highest-ranking Black executives in aerospace; named 2022 Black Engineer of the Year.

breakthroughDetail.d: Served as Boeing's CIO, CEO of Boeing Global Services, then CEO of Boeing Defense, Space & Security (2022–2024).
Won the award in 2022.

legacyDetail.d: The Morehouse dual-degree engineering track he used is a key pathway for Black engineers into Fortune 500 leadership.

sources.label: Black Engineer — 2022 Black Engineer of the Year

connections.label: CEO, Defense, Space & Security 2022–2024; earlier CIO and CEO of Global Services

name: Moss H. Kendrix
hbcuStory: Studied history, political science and economics at Morehouse, edited the Maroon Tiger and co-founded the Delta Phi Delta journalism society, through which he launched National Negro Newspaper Week in 1939.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up near Atlanta University in west Atlanta's Beaver Slide neighborhood, raised partly by his uncle, a local businessman.
breakthrough: In 1948 founded The Moss Kendrix Organization in Washington, D.C., with the motto "Court the Negro Market and Count the Results!"; Coca-Cola became his signature client.
legacy: Pioneered mainstream advertising featuring and targeting African American consumers for Coca-Cola, Carnation and Ford.

breakthroughDetail.d: The Moss Kendrix Organization served major corporate clients.
Best known for Coca-Cola advertising aimed at Black consumers.

legacyDetail.d: Educated corporations about Black buying power at a time when few did.

sources.label: Museum of Public Relations — Black PR pioneers

name: Harold Martin Jr.
hbcuStory: A 2002 Morehouse graduate who later returned as the college's interim president in 2017.
humbleBeginnings: Went on from Morehouse to an MBA at Harvard Business School and a J.D. at Yale Law School.
breakthrough: Became an associate partner at McKinsey & Co. in its higher-education practice before leading Morehouse, then became CEO of the Atlanta sports-bar chain Taco Mac.
legacy: Leads a regional restaurant chain with locations in Georgia and Tennessee.

breakthroughDetail.d: Runs the Atlanta-based chain of sports bars.
Led Morehouse on an interim basis in 2017.

legacyDetail.d: Moved from consulting to running a consumer business.

sources.label: The Atlanta Voice — Taco Mac's Harold Martin Jr.

name: Karim Webb
hbcuStory: Attended Morehouse College in Atlanta.
humbleBeginnings: Son of McDonald's executive-turned-franchisee Reggie Webb; worked in the family's 16-restaurant business from age 11.
breakthrough: With partner Edward Barnett formed PCF Management and raised about $6 million from individual investors during the recession to open Buffalo Wild Wings franchises, including the first full-service restaurant in South Los Angeles since the 1992 riots.
legacy: Won Black Enterprise's 2014 Franchise Company of the Year; his model trains local workers and youth in management and life skills.

breakthroughDetail.d: Bank financing was unavailable, so he raised roughly $6 million from individuals for two restaurants.
PCF Management named 2014 Franchise Company of the Year.

legacyDetail.d: Extended his father's McDonald's franchising legacy into a new brand.

sources.label: Franchise Times — Buffalo Wild Wings franchisee of fresh starts

name: Leroy Haynes
hbcuStory: A Morehouse graduate nicknamed "Roughouse" from his football days.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Clinton, Kentucky; briefly played for the Negro league Atlanta Black Crackers and served in the U.S. Army in Europe (1946–49).
breakthrough: Stayed in Paris after his service and, with his French wife Gabrielle, opened Gabby and Haynes and then Chez Haynes, which became a celebrated soul-food restaurant visited by famous entertainers.
legacy: Called America's 'unofficial ambassador to France for down home cooking'; his widow ran Chez Haynes for 23 years after his death until 2009.

breakthroughDetail.d: Iconic Paris soul-food restaurant.
Appeared in European gangster films from the 1960s.

legacyDetail.d: The restaurant stayed open until 2009 under his widow.

sources.label: Cuisine Noir — Leroy Haynes and Chez Haynes

name: Munson Steed
hbcuStory: Graduated from Morehouse College with a bachelor's degree in political science; in 2024 hosted the first Black Artificial Intelligence Conference at Morehouse.
humbleBeginnings: Built his company from Atlanta's local Black media scene.
breakthrough: Founded Steed Media Group, publisher of Rolling Out (founded 1998), a free weekly urban lifestyle magazine distributed in more than 19 cities.
legacy: Expanded Steed Media from print into digital, branded content, video and events; Rolling Out is among the largest Black-owned lifestyle publications.

breakthroughDetail.d: Free weekly lifestyle and entertainment magazine aimed at African American readers.
Distributed in over 19 U.S. cities.

legacyDetail.d: Has advocated for corporate ad spending with Black-owned media.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Rolling Out's Munson Steed

name: Shakir Stewart
hbcuStory: Graduated from Morehouse College (1996) and used money earned throwing parties as a student to build a small studio with friends.
humbleBeginnings: A native of Oakland, California.
breakthrough: Rose through the record business to Def Jam, becoming executive vice president of Def Jam and senior vice president of Island Def Jam Music Group.
legacy: Died at 34 in 2008; remembered as one of the most powerful young executives in hip-hop.

breakthroughDetail.d: Executive VP of Def Jam and SVP of Island Def Jam at his death.
Financed his first studio with college party-promotion money.

legacyDetail.d: Helped make Atlanta a center of label A&R.

sources.label: Los Angeles Times — Shakir Stewart obituary

connections.label: EVP, Def Jam; SVP, Island Def Jam

name: Steven Victor
hbcuStory: Attended Morehouse from 1998 to 2002, graduating with a bachelor's degree in English and psychology.
humbleBeginnings: Of Haitian descent.
breakthrough: Became chief creative officer of Kanye West's GOOD Music in 2015 and SVP of A&R at Universal Music Group, then founded his own label, Victor Victor Worldwide, in 2016.
legacy: Victor Victor signed Pop Smoke; Victor is a Billboard 40 Under 40 power player.

breakthroughDetail.d: Launched his own label in 2016.
Named chief creative officer of GOOD Music in 2015.

legacyDetail.d: Moved from salaried A&R to label ownership.

sources.label: Billboard — Steven Victor SVP A&R at UMG

name: Killer Mike
hbcuStory: Briefly attended Morehouse College in 1995, where he met producers The Beat Bullies and then Big Boi of Outkast.
humbleBeginnings: Born Michael Render to teenage parents and partly raised by his grandparents in Atlanta's Collier Heights neighborhood.
breakthrough: Debuted on Outkast's Stankonia (2000) and later won Grammys; in October 2020 co-founded Greenwood, a digital bank for Black and Latino customers, with Bounce TV founder Ryan Glover and Andrew Young.
legacy: Greenwood drew 500,000 sign-ups within months; Render is a prominent advocate for Black-owned business and banking.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-founded the Atlanta-based digital bank in 2020.
Greenwood reported 500,000 prospective members by January 2021.

legacyDetail.d: Uses his platform to push deposits into Black-owned institutions.

sources.label: CNN — Killer Mike's new Black-owned bank

name: Martin Luther King III
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in political science from Morehouse in 1979 — the school his father, grandfather and great-grandfather attended.
humbleBeginnings: Eldest son of Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King.
breakthrough: Led the SCLC (1997–2004) and in 2011 was among the co-founders of Bounce TV, a broadcast network aimed at Black audiences.
legacy: Continues his parents' human-rights advocacy through the Drum Major Institute.

breakthroughDetail.d: Part of the founding ownership group with Andrew Young, Rob Hardy and Will Packer.

legacyDetail.d: Fourth generation of his family to attend Morehouse.

name: Ras Asan Olugbenga
hbcuStory: Graduated cum laude from Morehouse College in 2013, then built the Mogul Minds wealth-building curriculum with classmates.
humbleBeginnings: Born Derric James Studamire in Cleveland, Ohio.
breakthrough: Co-founded BREAUX Capital with Morehouse classmate Derrius Quarles, a fintech focused on Black men's financial health, plus Million Dollar Scholar and Techgroove Fest under BREAUX and Company.
legacy: Recognized by Black Enterprise as a social entrepreneur.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-founded the financial technology company serving Black men.
Grew the businesses through accelerator programs.

legacyDetail.d: Teaches middle- and high-school students wealth building via business and investing.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Social entrepreneur Ras Asan Olugbenga

name: Derrius Quarles
hbcuStory: First-generation college student who graduated cum laude from Morehouse, studying sociology, biology and public health.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in the Bronzeville neighborhood on Chicago's South Side; won over $1.1 million in scholarships before college.
breakthrough: Co-founded and led BREAUX Capital, a fintech serving Black men, and Million Dollar Scholar, an education company.
legacy: Author and Roddenberry Foundation fellow focused on economic equity.

breakthroughDetail.d: Secured more than $1.1 million in scholarship awards.
Co-founder and former CEO.

legacyDetail.d: BREAUX built on behavioral economics research he led at Penn's Graduate School of Education.

sources.label: UrbanGeekz — 10 Black founders leading fintech firms

name: Metro Boomin
hbcuStory: Moved from St. Louis to Atlanta in 2012 to attend Morehouse, studying business management, while producing for Atlanta artists; left to pursue music.
humbleBeginnings: Born Leland Tyler Wayne in St. Louis; began producing as a teenager.
breakthrough: Became one of hip-hop's most influential producers (Future, 21 Savage, Migos, Drake, The Weeknd) and launched his own label, Boominati Worldwide.
legacy: Releases through Boominati Worldwide in partnership with Republic Records.

breakthroughDetail.d: His own label/imprint.
Produced multiple No. 1 albums and singles.

legacyDetail.d: Moved from work-for-hire production to label ownership.

sources.label: Billboard — Metro Boomin's Boominati Worldwide label

name: R. Roosevelt Thomas Jr.
hbcuStory: Graduated summa cum laude in mathematics from Morehouse in 1966 and returned to teach economics, finance and accounting; later dean of the business school at Clark Atlanta University.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Chattanooga, Tennessee, graduating from Howard High School in 1962.
breakthrough: After a University of Chicago MBA and Harvard D.B.A., he taught at Harvard Business School and founded the American Institute for Managing Diversity, consulting to large corporations and agencies.
legacy: Known as the "father of diversity" management; wrote seven books on the subject.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founder and first president of the American Institute for Managing Diversity.
Assistant professor at Harvard Business School until 1978.

legacyDetail.d: Recognized as a pioneer of the global diversity-consulting industry.

name: Robert E. Johnson
hbcuStory: Graduated from Morehouse College in 1948 (a classmate of Martin Luther King Jr.), then earned a master's in journalism at Syracuse.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Montgomery, Alabama.
breakthrough: Joined Jet in 1953, two years after its founding, and became its associate publisher and executive editor at Johnson Publishing Company.
legacy: Shaped Jet's civil-rights coverage for four decades and traveled in the 1972 presidential press corps.

breakthroughDetail.d: Associate publisher and executive editor of Jet.

legacyDetail.d: Jet's coverage under his editorship documented the civil rights era.

sources.label: NPR — Ebony/Jet founder John H. Johnson

name: Albert W. Dent
hbcuStory: Graduated from Morehouse in 1926 with an accounting degree, working at Atlanta Life Insurance Company while a student.
humbleBeginnings: Worked at Atlanta Life Insurance while still a student.
breakthrough: After serving as a branch office auditor for Atlanta Life, he became business administrator of New Orleans' Black-owned Flint-Goodridge Hospital and then president of Dillard University (1941–1969).
legacy: Built Dillard and Flint-Goodridge into pillars of Black New Orleans health care and education.

breakthroughDetail.d: Took a job as branch office auditor for Atlanta Life after graduating.
Led Dillard University for 28 years.

legacyDetail.d: Expanded hospital care for poor Black patients in New Orleans.

name: John Wesley Dobbs
hbcuStory: Attended Morehouse College for two years but left without graduating to care for his mother.
humbleBeginnings: Born and raised in Atlanta; spent decades as a federal railway mail clerk.
breakthrough: Known as the unofficial "mayor" of Sweet Auburn — which he called the "richest Negro street in the world" — he co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League with A. T. Walden.
legacy: All six of his daughters graduated from Spelman, including opera star Mattiwilda Dobbs; grandson Maynard Jackson became Atlanta's first Black mayor.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League.
Promoted Auburn Avenue's Black business district.

legacyDetail.d: His grandson Maynard Jackson became mayor of Atlanta in 1974.

sources.label: New Georgia Encyclopedia — John Wesley Dobbs

name: William Alexander Scott II
hbcuStory: A Morehouse graduate.
humbleBeginnings: Worked as the only Black clerk on the Jacksonville–Washington rail line and published Black business directories for Jacksonville (1927) and Atlanta.
breakthrough: Founded the Atlanta World on August 5, 1928 at age 26; it became a daily in 1931–32 — the first Black daily of the 20th century — and he built the first chain of Black newspapers, which peaked at about 50 titles.
legacy: Murdered in 1934; his brother C. A. Scott ran the Atlanta Daily World for decades from its Auburn Avenue offices.

breakthroughDetail.d: The Atlanta Daily World became a daily in 1932.
Added the Chattanooga Tribune and Memphis World in 1931, starting the first Black newspaper chain.

breakthrough: Owned and ran the Birmingham Black Barons (1939–1952) while managing T. H. Hayes & Sons Funeral Home and ventures in insurance, hotels, restaurants and nightclubs.
legacy: Hayes & Sons became the oldest Black-owned business in Memphis.

breakthroughDetail.d: Owner and president of the Birmingham Black Barons, 1939–1952.

legacyDetail.d: Family funeral home became Memphis's oldest Black-owned business.

name: Richard R. Wright Sr.
hbcuStory: Attended the Storrs School, which became Atlanta University, and graduated in its first college class (1876).
humbleBeginnings: Born into slavery in Dalton, Georgia; famous as the boy who told General O. O. Howard to 'tell them we are rising.'
breakthrough: After serving as founding president of the Georgia State Industrial College (now Savannah State) from 1891, he moved to Philadelphia in 1921, studied at Wharton at age 67 and founded the Citizens and Southern Bank and Trust Company.
legacy: His bank was the only Black-owned bank in the North at the time and the first Black trust company; he also founded National Freedom Day.

breakthroughDetail.d: Opened Citizens and Southern Bank and Trust on South Street in Philadelphia in 1921.
Enrolled to prepare for the banking venture.

legacyDetail.d: Ran the bank with family members until his death in 1947.

name: Lucy Craft Laney
hbcuStory: Entered Atlanta University's first class in 1869 and graduated from its normal department in 1873.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Macon, Georgia; her father had bought his freedom.
breakthrough: Founded the Haines Normal and Industrial Institute in Augusta in 1883 and led it for 50 years.
legacy: Her portrait hangs in the Georgia State Capitol; she trained generations of Black teachers.

breakthroughDetail.d: Opened the school in 1883 and won Presbyterian backing.

sources.label: New Georgia Encyclopedia — Lucy Craft Laney

name: James Weldon Johnson
hbcuStory: Completed Atlanta University's preparatory and college programs, graduating in 1894; won its oratory prize in 1892.
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Jacksonville, Florida, by a headwaiter father and teacher mother.
breakthrough: Co-wrote "Lift Every Voice and Sing" with his brother, served as U.S. consul in Venezuela and Nicaragua, and led the NAACP as executive secretary.
legacy: Author of The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man and God's Trombones.

breakthroughDetail.d: First Black executive secretary of the NAACP (1920).

name: Walter White
hbcuStory: Graduated from Atlanta University's high school in 1912 and the university in 1916; both parents were AU alumni.
humbleBeginnings: Son of an Atlanta postal worker; witnessed the 1906 Atlanta race massacre.
breakthrough: Investigated lynchings for the NAACP, often passing as white, and led the organization for a quarter century (1931–1955).
legacy: Oversaw the NAACP's legal campaign that led to Brown v. Board of Education.

breakthroughDetail.d: Executive secretary 1931–1955.

name: Fletcher Henderson
hbcuStory: Graduated from Atlanta University in 1920 with a degree in chemistry and mathematics.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Cuthbert, Georgia, to an educator father; moved to New York intending to study chemistry at Columbia.
breakthrough: Worked as a song demonstrator at Pace and Handy, then followed Harry Pace to Black Swan Records as musical director (1921–23).
legacy: His orchestra and arrangements laid the foundation for swing; he later arranged for Benny Goodman.

breakthroughDetail.d: 1921–1923, touring with Ethel Waters.

name: Ralph Abernathy
hbcuStory: Earned an M.A. in sociology with high honors from Atlanta University in 1951, after a mathematics degree from Alabama State.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up on a farm in Linden, Alabama.
breakthrough: Co-organized the Montgomery bus boycott with Martin Luther King Jr. and co-founded the SCLC.
legacy: Succeeded King as SCLC president (1968–1977).

breakthroughDetail.d: Led the SCLC after King's assassination.

name: Amy Sherald
hbcuStory: Began at Clark Atlanta on a pre-med track, cross-registered for painting at Spelman under Arturo Lindsay, and graduated with a B.A. in painting (1997).
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Columbus, Georgia.
breakthrough: Painted Michelle Obama's official portrait for the National Portrait Gallery (2018).
legacy: Her paintings now command major auction prices and museum retrospectives.

breakthroughDetail.d: Unveiled in 2018.

sources.label: The New Yorker — The Amy Sherald effect

name: Hosea Williams
hbcuStory: Earned his high-school diploma at 23 after World War II, then a bachelor's in chemistry from Morris Brown and a master's in chemistry from Atlanta University.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Attapulgus, Georgia; wounded in World War II.
breakthrough: Worked as a USDA research chemist in Savannah (1952–63) before becoming a top SCLC field general, leading the 1965 'Bloody Sunday' march in Selma with John Lewis.
legacy: In 1976 founded the Southeast Chemical Manufacturing and Distributing Company, selling specialized cleaning supplies, and served on the Atlanta City Council and in the Georgia Senate; started Hosea Feed the Hungry.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-led the Edmund Pettus Bridge march in 1965.
Founded Southeast Chemical Manufacturing and Distributing Co. in 1976.

name: Beverly Harvard
hbcuStory: Graduated from Morris Brown College with a B.A. in sociology at 22.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Macon, Georgia, graduating from Ballard-Hudson High School.
breakthrough: Rose through the Atlanta Police Department and became chief in 1994 — the first Black woman to lead a major U.S. city's police force.
legacy: Oversaw policing for the 1996 Atlanta Olympics.

breakthroughDetail.d: First Black woman police chief of a major U.S. city.

name: Charles P. Howard Sr.
hbcuStory: Attended Morris Brown College (and Tuskegee) after World War I, then earned his law degree at Drake University.
humbleBeginnings: Commissioned as a second lieutenant from the Fort Des Moines Black officers' training camp in 1917.
breakthrough: Founded the Iowa Observer, a multi-state Black newspaper, and the Howard News Syndicate, and co-founded the National Negro Publishers Association and the National Bar Association (1925).
legacy: Later served as a United Nations correspondent and civil rights activist.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founded the Iowa Observer and Howard News Syndicate.
Co-founded the National Negro Publishers Association.

legacyDetail.d: Co-founder of the National Bar Association.

name: J. D. Grier
hbcuStory: Earned a sociology degree at Morris Brown College, then a master of divinity at Gammon Theological Seminary (senior sermon, 1956).
humbleBeginnings: From Henry County, Georgia.
breakthrough: Served two terms in the Georgia House of Representatives (1965–68) among the first Black legislators since Reconstruction.
legacy: An SCLC leader who chaired the Atlanta Personnel Board.

breakthroughDetail.d: Among the first Black members of the Georgia House since Reconstruction.

name: Frank Yerby
hbcuStory: Graduated from Augusta's Haines Institute in 1933 and from Paine College with a B.A. in 1937, publishing poetry in the student paper; then earned an M.A. at Fisk.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Augusta, Georgia, to a mixed-race family.
breakthrough: His 1946 novel The Foxes of Harrow made him the first African American to write a bestselling novel and to have a book bought by a Hollywood studio.
legacy: Wrote 33 novels selling tens of millions of copies.

breakthroughDetail.d: The Foxes of Harrow (1946), filmed in 1947.

name: Joseph Lowery
hbcuStory: After studying at Knoxville College and Alabama A&M, he graduated from Paine College.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Huntsville, Alabama.
breakthrough: A United Methodist minister, he co-founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference with Martin Luther King Jr. and led it from 1977 to 1997.
legacy: Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2009; called the 'dean of the civil rights movement.'

breakthroughDetail.d: Led the organization for two decades.

name: Mike Thurmond
hbcuStory: Graduated cum laude from Paine College with a B.A. in philosophy and religion, then earned a J.D. at the University of South Carolina.
humbleBeginnings: Raised as a sharecropper's son in Clarke County, Georgia.
breakthrough: First Black legislator from Clarke County since Reconstruction (1986); Georgia Labor Commissioner (1999–2011).
legacy: Later CEO of DeKalb County and interim superintendent of DeKalb schools.

breakthroughDetail.d: Ran Georgia's labor department for 12 years.

name: Shannon Sharpe
hbcuStory: Played football and basketball and ran track at Savannah State, where his jersey is retired; drafted by Denver in 1990.
humbleBeginnings: Raised by his grandmother in rural Glennville, Georgia, alongside brother Sterling Sharpe.
breakthrough: Won three Super Bowls as a tight end and entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame (2011), then moved into TV analysis.
legacy: Built the Club Shay Shay podcast into a leading sports-and-culture show, joining Colin Cowherd's The Volume network in 2023 under a multi-year deal; won a 2025 NAACP Image Award.

breakthroughDetail.d: Considered one of the greatest tight ends.

humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Savannah's Old Fort neighborhood near Emmet Park and attended Beach High School.
breakthrough: Co-owned, with friend James Holmes, the Olympic Sports shop in downtown Savannah, and was elected to the Chatham County Commission in 1985.
legacy: Savannah's Joe Murray Rivers Jr. Intermodal Transit Center is named for him in honor of his transit advocacy.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-owned a downtown Savannah sporting goods store.

name: W. W. Law
hbcuStory: Led the NAACP Youth Council while a student at Georgia State College (now Savannah State), returning after WWII on the GI Bill to finish a B.S. in biology.
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Savannah; worked for decades as a U.S. mail carrier.
breakthrough: As president of the Savannah NAACP (1950–76) he led the Savannah Protest Movement that desegregated the city through nonviolent boycotts.
legacy: Founded Black history museums and preservation efforts in Savannah.

breakthroughDetail.d: Led the branch from 1950 to 1976.

humbleBeginnings: Born in Toccoa, Georgia.
breakthrough: Became the first associate director of the Georgia Democratic Party (1974) and the first Black chief administrator for a U.S. senator (Sam Nunn).
legacy: As chairman and CEO of 100 Black Men of America for about 20 years he raised nearly $100 million; founded the National Black College Alumni Hall of Fame and chaired Grady Hospital's board.

name: Rayfield Wright

legacy: Inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2006.

breakthroughDetail.d: Inducted 2006.

name: Shirley Sherrod
hbcuStory: Attended Fort Valley State College and later studied sociology at Albany State while organizing for SNCC, then earned a master's at Antioch.
humbleBeginnings: Her father, a farmer and church deacon, was shot dead by a white farmer in 1965 when she was 17.
breakthrough: Co-built New Communities, the pioneering Black farmers' land trust in southwest Georgia, and became Georgia's USDA Rural Development director.
legacy: Now leads the Southwest Georgia Project and New Communities at Cypress Pond; James Beard Leadership Award winner (2018).

breakthroughDetail.d: Black farmers' land trust in southwest Georgia.

name: Alice Coachman
hbcuStory: After a dressmaking degree from Tuskegee Institute (1946), she earned a B.S. from Albany State College.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in segregated Albany, Georgia, training on dirt roads and makeshift bars.
breakthrough: Won the high jump at the 1948 London Olympics, becoming the first Black woman to win Olympic gold.
legacy: Became one of the first Black athletes to endorse an international product (Coca-Cola) and founded a foundation for young athletes.

breakthroughDetail.d: London 1948 high jump.

name: Jo Marie Payton

humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Miami, graduating from Miami Carol City Senior High School in 1968.
breakthrough: Starred as Harriette Winslow on Family Matters (1989–1997), a role she originated on Perfect Strangers.
legacy: Voices Suga Mama on Disney's The Proud Family.

breakthroughDetail.d: Lead role for nine seasons.

name: Regina Benjamin

breakthrough: Ran a nonprofit rural health clinic in Bayou La Batre, Alabama, rebuilding it after hurricanes, and won a MacArthur 'genius' grant.
legacy: Served as the 18th U.S. Surgeon General (2009–2013).
